newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Indonesia happy at economic call to Moslem states.
newsitem.headline: Indonesia happy at economic call to Moslem states.

text.p: Indonesia said on Thursday it was satisfied with the response to its call for closer economic cooperation and trade between Islamic nations pressed during the annual meeting of Islamic nations.

"The time has come for us...to put more stress on our economic cooperation...this, I think, is one of the major themes that characterised this conference," Indonesian Foreign Minister Ali Alatas told reporters at the foreign ministers' meeting of the Organisation of the Islamic Conference (OIC).

The 24th OIC ministerial meeting ended the substantive part of its work on Thursday with the election of former Moroccan Prime Minister Azeddine Laraki as the new secretary-general of the 54-nation group.
He succeeds eight-year incumbent Hamid Algabid of Niger, who is currently a candidate for the post of U.N. secretary-general.

Alatas stressed that economics should not eclipse important political issues such as Bosnia-Herzegovina and Palestine, which topped the agenda during the five-day meeting. Other issues included Afghanistan, Somalia and Jammu and Kashmir.
Ministers decided to leave Kabul's seat vacant while urging the warring Afghan sides to form a government of national unity.
The conference ends on Friday with a final communique and an address by host minister Alatas.

Conference sources said Islamic states were expected to press U.N. Security Council members to push forward the Middle East peace process and counter what they see as Israel's reneging on agreements with the Palestinians.
Sources said a Kuwaiti attack on Iraq had been avoided in resulutions in the political affairs committee.

Kuwait's state minister of cabinet affairs, Abdul Aziz al-Dakheel, told a news conference his country had sought OIC support for the return of 600 people, mainly civilians, he said were still missing after Iraq's 1990 invasion of the Gulf state.

Kuwait was also seeking $107 billion in compensation from Iraq for damages suffered during the invasion, although this did not include the cost of environmental damage or the loss of oil revenue during the Iraqi occupation.
Alatas said Islamic states already had the institutions and mechanisms for economic cooperation, development and investment.
"What we are going to try to do is now to find out why it doesn't work...why it can't be more productive than it is now," he said.

"We should now focus on this part of our relations, namely economic cooperation, trade, mutual investment in each other, the transfer of technology and technical cooperation etc, making full use of our institutions," he said.

Another theme at the start of the conference was ways in which the Moslem community could counteract what it sees as frequent misrepresentation in Western states equating Islam with violence and terrorism.

Alatas said the meeting had not produced any concrete proposals, but he added: "We should do our utmost to make sure that there is a dissemination about what Islam really is about and what it isn't -- those efforts continue."
